# The System V Calling Sequence {#appendix-m-the-system-v-calling-sequence}

This appendix was added in this edition.
[Chapter 4](04-all-about-functions.qmd#assembly-language-functions-using-the-system-v-calling-convention)
explains the calling convention with integers and pointers only, which
is all this book\'s programs need. This appendix gives the rest of the
rules that Linux, the C library, Rust\'s `extern "C"` functions and
every compiler for x86-64 follow: where each kind of parameter goes,
how structures travel, how values come back, and what a function must
leave as it found it. They come from the
[System V ABI for x86-64][AM-ABI], which has every detail.

The Call, Step by Step {#the-call-step-by-step}
----------------------

The caller:

1.  Puts the parameters where they belong (see the next section):
    registers first, and the ones that don\'t fit in registers on the
    stack, pushed from the last one to the first, 8 bytes each (or a
    multiple of 8).

2.  Makes sure that _%rsp_ is a multiple of 16 when `call` runs. The
    `call` pushes the 8-byte return address, so *at the first
    instruction of a function, _%rsp_ + 8 is a multiple of 16*.

3.  For a function with a variable number of parameters (like
    `printf`), puts in _%al_ how many vector registers carry parameters
    (0 to 8).

4.  Runs `call`.

The function (the *callee*):

5.  Usually saves _%rbp_ and makes it the base of its stack frame, and
    moves _%rsp_ down to make room for its local variables, keeping it
    a multiple of 16 if it calls other functions.

6.  Saves every callee-saved register it uses (see
    [Saved Registers and State](#saved-registers-and-state)).

7.  Does its work, puts the return value in its place, restores what it
    saved, and runs `ret`.

Then the caller removes the parameters it pushed, if any (`addq` to
_%rsp_), and finds the return value.

Parameters {#parameters}
----------

Each parameter is put in a *class* by its type, and each class has its
own registers:

| Class | Types | Registers, in order |
|-------|-------|---------------------|
| INTEGER | Integers of every size, pointers, `bool`, `char` | _%rdi_, _%rsi_, _%rdx_, _%rcx_, _%r8_, _%r9_ |
| SSE | `float`, `double` (and vector types) | _%xmm0_ to _%xmm7_ |
| MEMORY | Structures bigger than 16 bytes, `long double` | None: on the stack |

The two lists are counted separately: in `f(int a, double b, int c)`,
`a` goes in _%rdi_, `b` in _%xmm0_ and `c` in _%rsi_. When a list runs
out, the parameters left go on the stack.

This program calls a function with eight integer parameters, so the
last two travel on the stack:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AM-01-sum8.s}
```

It returns 36. In gdb, at the first instruction of `sum8`, the stack
holds the return address, then the 7th parameter and the 8th:

```{.text check=appm-gdb-stack-parameters}
(gdb) break sum8
(gdb) run
(gdb) x/3gx $rsp
0x7ffcc2d5b648: 0x0000000000401033      0x0000000000000007
0x7ffcc2d5b658: 0x0000000000000008
(gdb) print (long)$rsp % 16
$1 = 8
```

_%rsp_ + 8 is a multiple of 16, as the rule says. After `pushq %rbp`
and `movq %rsp, %rbp`, the parameters are at `16(%rbp)` and `24(%rbp)`.

Structures {#structures}
----------

A structure of up to 16 bytes is cut into pieces of 8 bytes, called
*eightbytes*, and each piece is classified on its own: if it holds only
floating-point fields it is SSE, otherwise INTEGER. Each piece then
goes in the next register of its class, as if it were a parameter of
its own. If the registers aren\'t enough for all the pieces, the whole
structure goes on the stack. A structure bigger than 16 bytes always
goes on the stack: the caller copies it there.

This Rust program has one structure of each size, with
`#[repr(C)]` so that Rust lays them out as C would, and functions
declared `extern "C"` so that they follow this convention:

```{.rust .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AM-02-structs.rs}
```

`rustc --edition 2024 -C opt-level=2 --emit asm 0AM-02-structs.rs`
writes `0AM-02-structs.s`. The 16-byte `Pair` comes in two registers
and goes back in two:

```{.text check=appm-rust-swap-pair}
swap_pair:
        movq    %rsi, %rax
        movq    %rdi, %rdx
        retq
```

The 24-byte `Triple` is on the stack, above the return address
(`8(%rsp)` to `31(%rsp)`). To return it, the caller gives the function
the address of a place for the result as a hidden first parameter, in
_%rdi_, and the function returns that same address in _%rax_:

```{.text check=appm-rust-rotate-triple}
rotate_triple:
        movq    %rdi, %rax
        movups  16(%rsp), %xmm0
        movq    8(%rsp), %rcx
        movups  %xmm0, (%rdi)
        movq    %rcx, 16(%rdi)
        retq
```

(`movups` copies 16 bytes at once through _%xmm0_: the fields `b` and
`c` go to the first 16 bytes of the result, and `a` to its last 8.)

Return Values {#return-values}
-------------

| Return type | Where |
|-------------|-------|
| INTEGER, up to 8 bytes | _%rax_ |
| INTEGER, 9 to 16 bytes (a structure of two eightbytes) | _%rax_, then _%rdx_ |
| SSE | _%xmm0_, then _%xmm1_ |
| A structure with an INTEGER and an SSE eightbyte | _%rax_ and _%xmm0_ |
| MEMORY | In memory chosen by the caller, whose address arrives in _%rdi_; the function returns that address in _%rax_ |

Saved Registers and State {#saved-registers-and-state}
-------------------------

A function must return with these as they were when it was called:

-   The registers _%rbx_, _%rbp_, _%rsp_ and _%r12_ to _%r15_.

-   The direction flag, DF, which must be 0 when a function is called
    and when it returns.

-   The control bits of _MXCSR_ and the control word of the x87 unit
    (how floating-point numbers are rounded).

Every other register, including all the _%xmm_ registers and the other
flags, may be changed by the function. See
[Appendix L](appendix-l-registers-and-flags.qmd#general-purpose-registers)
for a table of every register.

The Red Zone {#the-red-zone}
------------

The 128 bytes below _%rsp_ are the *red zone*: Linux promises that
nothing else (a signal handler, for example) will write there. A
function that calls no other function can keep its local variables
there without moving _%rsp_ at all, and compilers do it to save two
instructions. The kernel itself can\'t rely on it, so it is compiled
without a red zone. The programs in this book always move _%rsp_, which
is never wrong.

The Frame Pointer {#frame-pointer-in-the-abi}
-----------------

The convention doesn\'t require _%rbp_ to point to the stack frame: it
is a callee-saved register like the others, and optimized code often
uses it for something else. Debuggers and profilers find their way up
the stack with tables that the compiler writes in the `.eh_frame`
section instead. See
[Chapter 12](12-optimization.qmd#chapter-12-optimization) for what the
frame pointer costs and what it gives.

System Calls Are Different {#system-calls-are-different}
--------------------------

The `syscall` instruction follows its own convention, which is close to
the one for functions but not the same:

-   The number of the call goes in _%rax_.

-   The parameters go in _%rdi_, _%rsi_, _%rdx_, _%r10_ (not _%rcx_),
    _%r8_ and _%r9_. There are never more than six, and never on the
    stack.

-   The result comes back in _%rax_. A value from -4095 to -1 is an
    error number, negated.

-   `syscall` itself overwrites _%rcx_ and _%r11_; the kernel keeps
    every other register.
